text:
The act of State doctrine means a domestic court treats a recognized foreign sovereign’s official public acts, done inside that sovereign’s own territory, as valid in the forum and leaves challenges to diplomacy or that state’s own legal system. Both listed formulations miss the rule: universal immunity is a separate doctrine, and a claim that domestic courts are well placed to try a state tort reverses this non-justiciability principle. It is strongest in United States law (Underhill v. Hernandez; Banco Nacional de Cuba v. Sabbatino) and appears in narrower strands in English law (Buttes Gas; Belhaj v. Straw).
